direct_answer: A lasting power of attorney (LPA) lets you choose people to make decisions for you if you lose mental capacity. In England and Wales, there are two types: property and financial affairs, and health and welfare. You must make one while you have capacity. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different systems.

content:
Planning ahead can give peace of mind. An LPA is one way to make sure decisions are made by people you trust.

This guide explains the basics and how to talk about it. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

The two types

  • Property and financial affairs: managing money, bills and property.
  • Health and welfare: decisions about care and treatment.

Making an LPA

In England and Wales, you can make an LPA online or on paper and register it with the Office of the Public Guardian. There is a fee, though reductions may be available. You must have capacity to make one.

Other UK nations

Scotland has its own power of attorney system through the Office of the Public Guardian (Scotland). Northern Ireland uses enduring powers of attorney. Get advice locally.

Starting the conversation

  • Choose a calm time.
  • Explain why it matters to you.
  • Talk about your wishes and values.
  • Involve family members as appropriate.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it too early?

It is best done while you are well.

Can I change my mind?

Yes, while you have capacity.
